name: School: Period Two
description: One optional roll per classroom, on the same terms as the morning. Not rolling is free. Failure buys extra work that costs a quarter; a critical failure costs a quarter and leaves them Fatigued. Both rooms pay off before the end of the episode and neither of them says so.

checks.name: Actually be able to do it, not just watch it done

dc.basis: level 1 standard DC 15. He is an outstanding teacher and the material is genuinely difficult -- the two cancel out

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Everything below, and the order to do it in: who is treated first when there are more casualties than hands. At the tram they can work on two people rather than one, and they will not waste the first minute deciding.
outcomes.success: They can stop bleeding with what is actually in their pockets, and they know which injuries get worse if the person is moved. Directly usable on the road below the gate.
outcomes.failure: They practise it wrong, confidently, until he stops them and makes them do it again properly. It takes the rest of the lesson and then some: one free quarter, and no lasting harm done to anything but the afternoon.
outcomes.criticalFailure: They get it wrong in a way that would have hurt somebody. He does not tell them so -- he takes his own coat off, puts their hands where they had them, and lets them feel exactly what they were about to do to a set of ribs, which on him is a very direct lesson. Nobody in that room forgets it. A quarter, and most of the evening: they begin the next day Fatigued.

bySkill.medicine: The direct route. He teaches it as procedure and they learn it as procedure.
bySkill.athletics: The physical half -- sustained pressure, and moving a heavier person without making the injury worse.
bySkill.crafting: Improvising the equipment. He is delighted by this and says so.
bySkill.nature: Knowing what a body does under stress, from having watched things bleed that were not people.

checks.name: Learn what can and cannot be required of you

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step easy. The Advocate wants them to have this and is actively helping -- the difficulty is caring enough to ask a second question

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Everything below, and the shape of the gap: every standing order that mentions the deep storage vaults points to an inventory nobody below the Commander may read. The Advocate does not draw the conclusion. They just stop talking for a second, and then carry on.
outcomes.success: Standing Order 14, paragraph 4 -- a direct instruction from a controlling officer -- and the three things a trainee is entitled to that nobody volunteers: to see the order, to have a reason recorded, and to say they do not understand.
outcomes.failure: They half-understand a clause and argue it, and are corrected completely, fairly, and without a trace of impatience -- which takes the rest of the lesson. Reading, due tomorrow: one free quarter.
outcomes.criticalFailure: They make it clear they think the whole subject is pointless, which is the one thing in this room that is not tolerated. The Advocate does not argue. They set the entire charter, annotated, and explain exactly why, once. A quarter and most of the night: their attitude to that character drops one step, from Friendly to Indifferent. They go on teaching exactly as well and will still answer anything asked. What stops is the unprompted half -- the aside, the paragraph read out because somebody ought to hear it, the thing said quietly on the way out of the room.

bySkill.society: The direct route. How an institution's rules actually get used, as opposed to what they say.
bySkill.diplomacy: Getting the Advocate onto what they themselves have been refused, which is where the vaults come up at all.
bySkill.computers: Reading the order index rather than the orders -- which ones have been amended, and how often.
bySkill.legal-lore: Reading the standing orders as legal instruments, which is the only approach that reaches the critical success cleanly.

participants: Individually -- each player is in one room or the other
notes:
NOT ROLLING IS FREE, SAME AS THE MORNING. A player who sits quietly through a lesson pays nothing and has done an ordinary thing. Only offer the roll to somebody who engages.

RISKS ARE NOT ANNOUNCED. Neither teacher states what a good roll buys or a bad one costs. The currency is always the same -- a free quarter -- and they have already spent one at the board that morning.

FIELD MEDICINE PAYS AT THE TRAM, ON A BEAT THAT EXISTS FOR IT. First Contact has an optional `the-hurt-ones` beat and a `treat-the-injured` check (`data/challenges/c1e2-first-contact.json`). Success there is what this lesson is for; a critical success here lets them work two casualties instead of one. Without this lesson the beat still runs, at a higher DC and with a worse ceiling. Do not mention any of it here.

STANDING ORDERS PAYS IN THE DEPUTY DIRECTOR'S OFFICE. Standing Order 14, paragraph 4 is quoted in The Hammer. A player who has it knows exactly what is being invoked, and can say so. Do not mention it here.

THE CRITICAL SUCCESS ON STANDING-ORDERS DOES NOT REVEAL WHAT IS IN THE VAULTS. It establishes only that orders about deep storage point to an inventory nobody below the Commander may read. The vaults hold recovered alien technology (LEDGER #40). The Advocate genuinely does not know what's in them.

SHUCKS IS ORDINARY HERE. No result in this room reveals anything about him. He is a doctor teaching a Tuesday class, and that unremarkableness is doing real structural work for the last scene of the episode.

PRICING AN INVENTED APPROACH. Standard Chapter One ladder: DC 13 if it costs them something real, DC 15 for the obvious way, DC 17 if it is free or skips a step, DC 20 if it would get more than the scene was going to give.
